project.name: vibecode-like-a-dev
project.title: Vibecode Like A Dev
project.idea: A deterministic compiler for engineering discipline. A developer who can describe an app in one paragraph, or point at a repository they already have, runs it and gets a specification packet an agent can execute: requirements with acceptance criteria, a computed rigor tier, the gates that define done, and a script that fails CI when the spec and the code stop agreeing. Today those developers paste a prompt into an agent and inherit whatever engineering the model happened to infer, which is why the output rarely survives review, maintenance or a second contributor.

primitives.title: Product brief
primitives.why: An agent fills every ambiguity silently. A written brief is the cheapest place to remove ambiguity.

primitives.title: Non-goals and scope discipline
primitives.why: Scope creep is the default failure mode of generated code; explicit non-goals are the brake.

primitives.title: Ubiquitous language and DDD basics
primitives.why: Shared vocabulary is the highest-leverage defence against plausible-but-wrong generated code.

primitives.title: Test-driven loop
primitives.why: A failing test is the only instruction an agent cannot misinterpret.

primitives.title: Acceptance criteria and traceability anchors
primitives.why: Requirement-to-test anchors are the mechanism that closes the enforcement gap.

primitives.title: Agent handoff packet
primitives.why: The spec is useless if the agent that receives it cannot find the entry point.

primitives.title: Aggregates and invariants
primitives.why: Invariants are the properties mutation and property-based tests verify.

primitives.title: Architecture style selection
primitives.why: Default to a modular monolith; distributed complexity must be justified, not inherited.

primitives.title: Secrets and supply chain hygiene
primitives.why: Leaked keys and unpinned dependencies are the two cheapest attacks on a new product.

primitives.title: CI gates from the first commit
primitives.why: A gate that does not run in CI is a suggestion.

primitives.title: User journeys as testable slices
primitives.why: Journeys turn a paragraph of intent into testable slices.

primitives.title: Bounded contexts and module seams
primitives.why: Context boundaries decide module seams before any file is generated.

primitives.title: Test budget and suite shape
primitives.why: Test suite shape must match risk: heavy on domain rules, thin on frameworks.

primitives.title: Automated review protocol
primitives.why: Self-review is theatre when the reviewer shares the author's blind spots.

primitives.title: Ports and adapters (hexagonal)
primitives.why: Keeping the domain free of framework and vendor code is what makes later replacement cheap.

primitives.title: Architecture decision records
primitives.why: Decisions without rationale get re-litigated on every agent session.

primitives.title: Build versus buy for commodity concerns
primitives.why: Most generated auth, billing and queues are worse than the boring proven option.

requirements.title: Runnable from a clean clone
requirements.statement: A new contributor can install dependencies, start the project and run its tests from a clean clone using only the documented commands, with no manual database seeding, no hidden local state and no undocumented environment variables.
requirements.failurePath: A missing environment variable produces a single actionable error naming the variable, not a stack trace deep in a startup path.

acceptance.text: Given a fresh clone and an empty environment file, when the documented setup command runs, then it either succeeds or lists every missing required variable by name.

requirements.title: The primary journey works end to end
requirements.statement: The single journey described in the product brief works from first step to last, through the real interface, persisting whatever it must persist, and produces the outcome the brief promises. It is exercised by one end-to-end test, not by unit tests of its parts.
requirements.failurePath: If any step of the journey fails, the user is left in a state they can retry from, with no partially written data and an explanation that names what failed.

acceptance.text: Given a new user and empty storage, when they complete the primary journey using only the documented interface, then the outcome named in the brief exists and is readable on a second visit.
Given the same journey, when a dependency it relies on is unavailable, then the user sees an actionable message and no partial record is created.

requirements.title: Explicit non-goals
requirements.statement: The product brief lists at least three things this version deliberately does not do, and the codebase contains no partially built version of them.
requirements.failurePath: Out-of-scope work arrives as a failing review comment referencing a non-goal, rather than as silent extra code.

acceptance.text: Given the brief, when a reviewer reads the change, then every capability in the diff maps to an in-scope requirement or is rejected.

requirements.title: Predictable command-line behaviour
requirements.statement: Commands follow a documented grammar, write data to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, support --help and --version, and exit non-zero on failure.
requirements.failurePath: An invalid flag prints usage to stderr and exits 2; a partial failure exits non-zero and leaves no half-written output file.

acceptance.text: Given an invalid flag, when the command runs, then usage goes to stderr, stdout is empty and the exit code is non-zero.

requirements.title: The product's own rules are named and pinned
requirements.statement: Every invariant listed in the domain model names a rule that makes this product itself, and each has at least one automated test whose failure mode is that rule being violated. An invariant with no test is a comment; a test that would pass with the rule inverted is not a test.
requirements.failurePath: If a core rule is inverted by a refactor, a test fails and names the rule, rather than the change being discovered by a user or a reviewer.

acceptance.text: Given the invariants listed in the domain model, when the suite runs, then each invariant is covered by a test that fails if its rule is inverted.
Given an invariant added to the domain model, when it has no test, then the review checklist rejects the change.

gates.statement: The project starts from a clean clone with one documented command.
Lint or typecheck runs in CI on every pull request.
One happy-path smoke test exercises the primary user journey.
The full test suite runs in CI on every pull request and is required to merge.
Every rule in the domain model has at least one automated test.
Every requirement marked automated maps to a named test through an @req anchor.
README documents how to run, test and deploy, plus known limitations.
No secret is committed; configuration comes from the environment and is validated at startup.
